children.text: Basco Lighthouse is a white, six-story lighthouse about 20 m tall that stands on Naidi Hills northwest of Basco, the main town of Batanes. From the fifth-floor viewing gallery you can see Mount Iraya, Basco Port and, on clear days, as far as Sabtang and Itbayat islands.

Basco Lighthouse stands on Naidi Hills in Barangay San Antonio, Basco, the capital of Batanes province. The white cylindrical tower with a red lantern and red trim often appears on Batanes postcards and tourism material. It is about
1.2 km

on foot from Basco Port, so if your lodging is in the town center you can walk up without a tricycle. It is commonly recommended as an easy first-day stop for travelers heading to the Philippines' northernmost islands. Batanes is the Philippines' northernmost island group, and Basco is the administrative and transport center of Batan Island. The whole island is made of low grassy hills, sea and the stone houses of the Ivatan people, so the view from the lighthouse feels like a miniature of all of Batanes.
The lighthouse is about
(66 ft) tall and has six floors. According to Wikipedia, its light has a range of about 10 nautical miles (about
19 km

) and flashes white once every four seconds. One trip report says you climb 54 steps to the viewing gallery on the fifth floor. The lamp at the top serves as a navigation aid for fishing boats and ships while the tower also functions as a tourist attraction. Beside it is a caretaker's house built in the traditional Ivatan stone-house style, and it is said to operate as a bed and breakfast.

The site was significant even before the lighthouse. The current lighthouse is said to have first been lit in 2003, and it was built on the site of Basco's first lighthouse and of American-period telegraph facilities. Those facilities were destroyed by Japanese bombing at the start of World War II. American-era bunkers and a historical marker remain on the hill, so reading the history here makes the visit much richer than just looking at the tower and heading back down. It was the first completed of three lighthouses (Basco, Sabtang and Mahatao) proposed by former Congressman Florencio Abad, who suggested they could also be used as tourist attractions.

This guide is for travelers who spend a day or half a day in Basco and want to see North Batan at an easy pace with the lighthouse as the centerpiece. Batanes is a place where flights are often cancelled and the weather changes fast, so the key is to leave slack in your schedule. The lighthouse itself takes about an hour at most, but pairing it with nearby Vayang Rolling Hills, views of Mount Iraya and Tukon Church in town makes a good half-day route. Admission fees and opening hours are not clearly stated in the sources, so confirm them locally. The Ivatan people here have long built houses of stone and lime to stand up to fierce winds and the sea, and the caretaker's house beside the lighthouse follows that tradition. Sit for a moment at the foot of the lighthouse and listen to the wind, and you start to understand why time moves so slowly on this island.

From the viewing gallery, reached by climbing 54 steps, you can see all of Batan Island, Basco town and Basco Port. On clear days Sabtang Island to the south and Itbayat Island to the north are said to be visible as well. Winds are often strong, so watch your hat and small belongings.

From Basco Lighthouse you get a close view of Mount Iraya, the active volcano in the north of Batan Island. Clouds often hide it, so going early in the morning gives you a better chance of a clear view.

The caretaker's house beside the lighthouse is modeled on a traditional Ivatan stone house. You can see the thick stone walls and low roof up close, and there are reports that it offers bed-and-breakfast lodging. Check directly on site about staying.

American-era bunkers and a marker remain on the hill. You can read the explanation that this was the site of Basco's first lighthouse and a telegraph facility, which was destroyed during World War II.
The hill is open, so early morning and the hour around sunset, when the sky changes color, are good for photos. The sea, grassland and white tower fit in one frame, so a wide-angle lens works well.

The way from the port to the lighthouse is a gentle uphill that is easy to walk, and Wikivoyage lists Naidi Hills as a sight within walking distance of Basco. Strolling slowly past grassland and sea views is a pleasure in itself.

Besides Basco Lighthouse, Batanes has Tayid Lighthouse in Mahatao (hexagonal), Sabtang Lighthouse and others. Because the same person proposed them, comparing their shapes is part of the fun. Basco Lighthouse is round and cylindrical.

items.title: Half-day North Batan route
items.subtitle: From the lighthouse to the coastal grasslands

children.text: Go from your Basco lodging to Naidi Hills on foot or by tricycle. Enjoy the cool early-morning air and soft light.
Climb to the fifth-floor viewing gallery of Basco Lighthouse and look out over Mount Iraya, the port and the sea.
Look around the American-era bunkers and the marker near the lighthouse, and walk the grassy hill.
Have breakfast at your lodging, then take a tricycle to Vayang Rolling Hills.
Continue to other North Batan sights such as Valugan Boulder Beach, and have lunch.
The lighthouse and Vayang Rolling Hills are close, about
10 minutes
by tricycle. Hotel staff can sometimes connect you with a driver.

items.title: Light arrival-day route
items.subtitle: An evening walk up from the port

children.text: Go from the airport to your lodging, unpack and rest. Basco is small, so most places are a short distance away.
Set out from the Basco Port area and walk up to Naidi Hills. The distance is about
1.2 km
Climb the lighthouse, enjoy the view around sunset and come down before dark.
Have dinner at a restaurant in town serving Ivatan dishes.
The hill road is dark after sunset and may have few streetlights, so bring a flashlight.
Take a domestic flight from Ninoy Aquino International Airport in Manila to Basco Airport (BSO). Wikipedia says PAL Express operates the Manila route.
Basco Airport handles only small turboprop aircraft. Flights are often cancelled in bad weather, so it is safer to leave extra days before your flight home.
Round-trip fares vary widely by season, and examples of about ₱10,000–20,000 have been reported. Check the airline's announcements.
There are reports that the visitor pre-registration system for Batanes changed in 2026. Check the Batanes provincial government's announcements before you leave.

From Basco Airport to lodging in town you take a short tricycle ride. Guides quote about ₱20–30 for town rides (a 2018 trip report lists about ₱30 in the town center and ₱50 to the outskirts); no official fare list was found, so agree the price with the driver before riding.
The lighthouse is about
1.2 km
on foot from Basco Port, so you can walk instead of taking a tricycle.
Tricycle tours of North Batan that combine the lighthouse, Vayang Rolling Hills, Valugan Boulder Beach and more were listed in 2019–2026 guides at about
per tricycle (for two people). There is no official fare list and fuel costs can shift prices, so confirm with your lodging or driver.
Some travelers rent a bicycle or motorbike and explore on their own.

Wikivoyage describes the best time for Batanes as the dry season, roughly March–June, when winds and waves calm down. In this period cancellations are less likely and planning is easier. Basco gets about 2,300 mm of rain a year, with August and September the wettest, and June and July are said to be the hottest months.

Batanes lies in the path of typhoons, and even without a typhoon strong winds can close roads and attractions. The lighthouse viewing gallery can be dangerous in strong wind, so check the weather before climbing.

Basco town has guesthouses and small hotels clustered together. Wikivoyage advises that Basco is the only place on Batan with banks, so bring plenty of cash. Town has restaurants and small shops serving Ivatan food, and on the lighthouse grounds there is said to be a café in a renovated old telegraph building. Operations change often, so check in advance.

Most ingredients in Batanes are imported, so food is known to be expensive. Seafood caught locally is sometimes cooked for you at your lodging. Coconut crab (about ₱800–2,000) is a dish that requires a permit, so eat it only at places that have one.
Early morning or around sunset the light is soft and there are fewer people. The midday sun is strong, so bring a hat and sunscreen.
Winds are often strong, so bring a hat with a strap and a light jacket. Watch your belongings near the railing of the viewing gallery.
Opening hours and admission fees are not in the sources. Ask your lodging staff or the Basco tourism office first.
The walk from the port is a continuous uphill, so wear comfortable shoes. There is no shade at midday, so bring water.
Vayang Rolling Hills is about
2.7 km
from the lighthouse, about
10 minutes
by tricycle, so it is easy to combine on the same day.
Phone signal and internet can be unreliable, so save maps offline. Bring plenty of cash as well.
The viewing gallery is narrow, so do not climb up and down all at once; take turns when taking photos.
On the way down, rest at a market or small shop near the port and try Ivatan snacks and drinks. Places are small and may have short opening hours.
Batanes has frequent typhoons and strong winds can close roads and attractions, and small-plane cancellations are common, so you need slack days before your flight home.
There is a risk of strong wind and falls near the gallery railing, so hold children's hands tightly.
The hill road is dark after sunset. Come down before dark or bring a flashlight.
Opening hours and entry rules for the lighthouse are not confirmed. If it is locked, do not force your way in.
There are reports that Batanes visitor rules, including pre-registration, are changing, so check official announcements before you go.
Bunkers and old structures may be worn, so do not climb on or lean against them.
An overview of the whole of Batan Island, including Basco, Mahatao, Ivana and Sabtang, with its rolling grassy hills and stone-house villages. Refer to it first when planning your trip.
Sabtang Island to the south is famous for its Ivatan stone-house villages. It is visible from the lighthouse on clear days, and you cross by morning boat from Radiwan Port in Ivana.
Green rolling hills about
2.7 km
from the lighthouse, roughly
10 minutes
by tricycle. Easy to combine on the same morning.
A round-boulder beach on Basco's east coast, about
3 km
from town. It is often visited together on the North Batan route.
